vignette:
Thea's Vigil

Thea was fifty-four when the cardiologist told her that the irregular heartbeat her internist had detected six months earlier was actually a serious arrhythmia-the kind that could stop her heart without warning. She remembered the exact moment: the doctor's face had a particular softness to it, the kind people use when delivering news they know will shatter something. He had explained the condition in measured tones, mentioned medication and monitoring, possibly an ablation procedure. She had nodded, asked a question or two, and then sat in her car in the hospital parking lot for two hours, unable to turn the key in the ignition. The smell of the garage-a mix of concrete and exhaust-had mixed with the memory of the antiseptic tang that clung to her clothes from the cardiology wing, and she had felt her chest tighten in the exact way the cardiologist had warned her about.

The months that followed were a slow unraveling. Thea had spent thirty years as an electrician, had rewired houses, installed systems in commercial buildings, had never been afraid of her body. Her body had been an instrument of competence. But now her body had become a traitor, a thing that might betray her at any moment. She began to notice her heartbeat constantly-a flutter, a skip, a surge when she climbed stairs or felt startled. Each irregularity sent a spike of fear through her. She started avoiding the very thing that might have helped: she stopped going to her follow-up appointments. The thought of sitting in that waiting room, breathing in that hospital smell, having a technician place sensors on her chest while she lay still and hyperaware of every pulse-it was unbearable. She told herself she would reschedule, but she never did.

At work, things began to slip. Thea had always been reliable, the electrician you called when the job was complicated. But six months into her diagnosis, she found herself declining jobs that involved ladders or heights. She told her boss it was her knees. The truth was that being elevated, working in tight spaces, exertion-all of it made her acutely aware of her breathing, and the moment she heard her own breath quicken, her mind would flash to the cardiologist's office. Her heart would race in response to the fear itself, and she would become convinced that this was it, this was the arrhythmia finally catching her. She had started turning down jobs so frequently that her boss had begun giving the better contracts to the younger electrician they had hired last year. By the anniversary of her diagnosis-a date she could not stop anticipating, dreading-Thea had lost two major clients and was working half the hours she used to.

She had also begun to mentally rewrite her life. Late at night, she would lie in bed and construct elaborate counterfactuals: if she had gone to the doctor sooner, if she had eaten differently, if she had not worked such long hours in her forties, if she had stayed married instead of divorcing fifteen years ago-perhaps her ex-husband would have noticed something was wrong, would have insisted she get checked. These thoughts consumed her in a way that felt almost protective, as if by imagining a different timeline, she could somehow undo the present one.

When her daughter called one evening and found Thea's voice flat and distant, she recognized something was wrong. Thea had been doing what she called "pretending"-a kind of mental stepping outside herself where she would observe her own fear from a distance, as though the diagnosis had happened to someone else entirely, someone she was watching from behind glass. It was a relief in the moment but left her feeling hollowed out afterward.

Three weeks ago, Thea's daughter had sat down with her and said, gently, that something had to change. Thea was not living anymore; she was hiding. That conversation had cracked something open. Thea had finally called a therapist, and in the intake, she had admitted the truth: she was terrified of her own body, terrified that seeking help would confirm her worst fears, and exhausted by the constant vigilance. What she wanted most was to feel safe in her own skin again. What she feared most was that she never would.
